about: Tree and bush layer of the world knowledge graph. The owner says trees look most fake. The cause is mostly structure, not leaf texture: real stands have many thin trunks of mixed size, an undergrowth layer, a closed 'wall' of branches at the forest edge, and mowed strips at the road. This file says, per place, what grows, how big, how dense, in which layers, and why (each value has a source in the data). Run time: the scan engine reads TreeMap, LANDFIRE, NLCD and lidar per tile and fills the TREE chunk (48 B per tree) and a layer mask for undergrowth and edge; the trees team makes the meshes.

what_changes_first_for_trees.change: Real stand from a real plot. Each 30 m TreeMap pixel points to one FIA plot, and that plot has a tree list: species, trunk diameter, height, crown ratio, live or dead, and trees per acre. We plant that list (trees per acre x 0.09 ha per pixel), with positions from lidar crowns where they exist and else from a spaced point process. Result: mixed sizes, mixed species, some dead snags, the right number of thin trunks.
what_changes_first_for_trees.fixes: every tree the same size; too few trunks; one species

what_changes_first_for_trees.change: Forest edge layer. Along a road through forest, the first 3-8 m of trees keep branches to the ground (they get side light) and a band of shrubs and young trees fills the gap; in the interior, trunks are bare up to the canopy base height (LANDFIRE CBH). Between the road and the edge, a mowed strip whose width comes from the road class (state mowing practice, roughly the clear zone).
what_changes_first_for_trees.fixes: you can see straight into the forest between bare trunks, which looks fake from the road

what_changes_first_for_trees.change: Undergrowth by forest group x region x slope aspect x moisture (table below), from LANDFIRE EVT where it names a shrub layer: rhododendron and mountain laurel thickets on north slopes and along streams in the Appalachians (US 129 Dragon), sword fern and salal in Pacific Northwest forests, saw palmetto under Florida pines, wiregrass under longleaf, bare needle litter under dense loblolly, open grass under ponderosa.

Street and yard trees sized by the age of the neighbourhood: tree height grows with years since the houses were built (NSI/ACS median year built), so a 2015 subdivision has 3-5 m trees and a 1925 street has 20-30 m trees over the road. Foundation shrubs along house fronts after about 1945; hedges and tree rows on lot lines.
what_changes_first_for_trees.fixes: new suburbs with old trees, old streets with no canopy

what_changes_first_for_trees.change: Season and colour from the date and place: leaf-out and leaf-fall by latitude and elevation, autumn colour by species group (maple red-orange, oak brown-red, aspen and birch yellow, conifers stay green), winter leaf-off opens the view through deciduous forest.

layers.from: TreeMap plot tree list (TreeMap 2016/2020/2022) + 3DEP lidar crowns (segmentation, proposal 4) + NLCD tree canopy cover as a density check
the smaller trees of the same plot list (diameter < 12.7 cm saplings are in FIA microplots) + LANDFIRE EVH height class
LANDFIRE EVT shrub types and the understory table below; cover from LANDFIRE EVC where EVT is a shrubland
litter type by forest group (needles, broad leaves, moss, grass), from this table; feeds the ground material and scatter
derived: the band within 3-8 m of where canopy meets a road, field or lawn

forest_type_groups.about: FIA forest-type groups (FORTYPCD // 10 * 10). Crown form drives the mesh family; heights come from the plot tree list, not from this table. Undergrowth entries are typical, confidence medium unless marked.

100.name: White / red / jack pine
100.crown: conical young, irregular flat-topped old (white pine)
100.undergrowth: low blueberry, bracken fern, needle litter

120.name: Spruce / fir
120.crown: narrow conical, branches to the ground at edges

140.name: Longleaf / slash pine
140.crown: tall clear trunk, small round crown on top
140.undergrowth: open: wiregrass and saw palmetto (fire kept); slash pine in Florida with palmetto

160.name: Loblolly / shortleaf pine
160.crown: oval crown on a long clear trunk; plantations in straight rows
160.undergrowth: needle litter, sweetgum and red maple saplings, greenbrier, Japanese honeysuckle at edges
160.plantation_rule: rows 2.5-3.7 m apart where the stand origin is planted (FIA STDORGCD) or the aerial shows rows

180.name: Pinyon / juniper
180.undergrowth: bare soil and gravel between trees, sagebrush, bunch grass, biological soil crust

200.name: Douglas-fir
200.undergrowth: west side: sword fern, salal, Oregon grape, moss on trunks; east side: drier, grass and ninebark

220.name: Ponderosa pine
220.crown: open, orange plated bark on big trees
220.undergrowth: open park-like grass and needle litter, scattered shrubs

280.name: Lodgepole pine
280.undergrowth: sparse, many dead standing trunks after beetle kill

300.name: Hemlock / Sitka spruce
300.undergrowth: moss everywhere, ferns, devil's club, nurse logs

340.name: Redwood
340.undergrowth: redwood sorrel, sword fern, tanoak; deep shade

370.name: California mixed conifer
370.undergrowth: manzanita and ceanothus on dry sides

400.name: Oak / pine
400.undergrowth: mixed shrubs, leaf and needle litter

500.name: Oak / hickory
500.undergrowth: Appalachian: rhododendron and mountain laurel on north slopes and near streams, dogwood and redbud in the subcanopy; Ozarks and Midwest: open, spicebush, poison ivy, leaf litter

600.name: Oak / gum / cypress
600.crown: broad; bald cypress with knees in water
600.undergrowth: wet: Spanish moss on oaks and cypress, palmetto, standing water

700.name: Elm / ash / cottonwood
700.rule: on the Great Plains this group follows rivers and creeks only (Nebraska); shelterbelt rows around farmsteads (eastern redcedar, cottonwood, green ash) are a separate planted layer

800.name: Maple / beech / birch
800.undergrowth: sparse under beech; hobblebush, ferns; stone walls in New England woods (old farm fields)

900.name: Aspen / birch
900.undergrowth: grass and forbs, dense young aspen

920.name: Western oak
920.undergrowth: golden dry grass in summer (California), poison oak

999.name: Nonstocked
999.undergrowth: LANDFIRE EVT decides (shrubland, grass, recent burn or cut)

non_forest.about: Where TreeMap has no forest, LANDFIRE EVT and NLCD decide the cover.
non_forest.shrubland_west: sagebrush (grey-green, 0.5-1.5 m) on the Great Basin and Wyoming; creosote bush (spaced 2-5 m apart, bare ground between) in the hot deserts; chaparral (dense, 1-3 m) on California slopes; coastal sage scrub on CA-1
non_forest.grassland_plains: mixed and tall grass; Sandhills grass on dunes (Cherry County); fence lines and windmills; trees only along water and around farmsteads
non_forest.pasture_hay: short grass, fences, single shade trees in fields (often oaks or cottonwoods), round bales in season
non_forest.crops: row direction from the aerial; field edge strip of grass and weeds 1-3 m
non_forest.wetland: cattail and reed along ditches and pond edges; standing water by season

roadside_profile.about: Cross-section from the pavement edge outwards. Widths come from the CORR cross-section where it exists; these are fallbacks.

mowed_strip_m.residential: lawn to the kerb or edge
mowed_strip_m.why: state DOTs mow about the clear zone near higher-speed roads; low roads get one mower width or none (confidence medium)

roadside_profile.power_line_corridor: where a pole line runs inside the forest, trees are cut back about 3-6 m each side of the wires (utility vegetation management) - a visible gap in the canopy along the road
roadside_profile.mountain_road: on cut slopes (lidar slope > 35 deg) show rock or thin soil with small trees and roots; on fill slopes, trees start lower and lean out

street_trees.where: planting strip between kerb and sidewalk where the cross-section has one; else in the front lawn 3-6 m from the edge
street_trees.spacing_why: common city street-tree spacing guidance (30-50 ft)
street_trees.age_rule: height = species max height x (1 - exp(-years since built / 25)) with years from the tract median year built; confidence low
street_trees.species: by region and hardiness zone (see below); one species per block is common on older planned streets (lumpiness high)

foundation_shrubs.where: along the building front, 0.5-1.5 m out
foundation_shrubs.why: post-war ranch and later houses are almost always planted along the front; confidence low

hedges_and_lot_rows.note: privet, arborvitae (north), wax myrtle and ligustrum (south)

midwest: ash (many dead or removed after emerald ash borer)
southwest_desert: gravel yards with cactus and agave (xeriscape)
hawaii: invasive strawberry guava and albizia in wet areas

season.leaf_out_rule: Hopkins' bioclimatic rule as fallback: spring events about 4 days later per degree of latitude north, per 5 degrees of longitude east, and per 400 ft (about 120 m) higher; replace with USA-NPN or satellite phenology when its terms are read

autumn_colour.conifer: stays green; larch and bald cypress turn orange and drop

season.winter: deciduous crowns become bare branches (the trees team needs a leaf-off mesh state); evergreen shrubs (rhododendron) stay; snow on branches in snowy climates by the weather

alaska_hawaii.alaska: TreeMap covers the lower 48 only, so Alaska uses LANDFIRE (which covers Alaska) and NLCD Alaska: boreal black spruce on cold wet ground (thin 'pencil' spruce, often leaning on permafrost), white spruce and birch on warm slopes and rivers, willow and alder thickets at the road edge, tundra above tree line and on the North Slope (Koppen ET); southeast Alaska is temperate rainforest (group 300). Held-out test places: Anchorage, Fairbanks North Star, Juneau.
alaska_hawaii.hawaii: TreeMap does not cover Hawaii; LANDFIRE covers Hawaii. Wet windward sides: dense green forest, many invasive trees (albizia, strawberry guava), tree ferns at higher elevation; dry leeward sides: kiawe and grass; lava flows: bare black rock (young) to ohia and fern (older); much of the lowland is former sugar and pineapple land, now grass and brush. Held-out test places: Honolulu, Hawaii County, Maui.
